entities.name: Adeimantus of Corinth
entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Adeimantus of Corinth, son of Ocytus (Ὠκύτος), emerged as a pivotal Corinthian commander during the momentous invasion of Greece by Xerxes I in 480 BCE, a conflict that pitted the vast Achaemenid Persian Empire against the fragmented city-states of ancient Greece. His actions and controversial counsel profoundly shaped the early naval strategies of the Hellenic League, particularly in the lead-up to the crucial naval engagements that would determine the fate of Hellenic resistance. As a representative of Corinth, a powerful maritime city-state with a significant fleet, Adeimantus played a critical role in the strategic deliberations of the allied Greek forces, advocating for the defense of the Peloponnese, a stance often at odds with the Athenian strategy of engaging the Persian fleet further north.

The core of Adeimantus's documented actions centers on the eve of the Battle of Artemisium in 480 BCE. Facing the overwhelming numerical superiority of the Persian fleet, and concerned for the safety of the Peloponnese, Adeimantus famously threatened to withdraw the Corinthian contingent, a significant portion of the allied fleet, from the northern defensive line. This near-defection, recorded by Herodotus, underscored the deep strategic divisions among the Greek allies, particularly between the Peloponnesian states and Athens, regarding where best to confront the Persian advance. His reluctance to commit fully to the northern defense, driven by a desire to protect the Isthmus of Corinth, highlighted the precarious unity of the Hellenic League.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Adeimantus's actions highlighted the critical internal divisions and strategic debates within the Hellenic League during the Persian Wars, influencing the early defensive posture of the Greek fleet at Artemisium. His role underscores the fragility of alliances even in the face of existential threats.
